boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen New Orleans record (April 25-May 1, 1862) in Expedition to, and Capture of, New Orleans [April-May 1862]. The passage of Forts Jackson and St. Philip (LA001) is context; its April 24 action and April 28 surrender are not counted here. Campaign-wide movements, the other exterior works and the evacuation of Pensacola are context; multi-action totals are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Department of the Gulf [US] and Department No. 1 [CS]; the live field reads zero. Lovell says every Confederate soldier but one company had gone to Corinth and the city was held by about 3,000 ninety-day troops, about 1,200 with muskets, against more than 100 guns afloat; on April 25 thirteen ships engaged the batteries five miles below the city, which Mahan says mounted five and nine guns. Mahan says 250 marines were landed on the 29th. No Union army strength is given in the inspected passages.
claims.rationale: Militia, ship and gun figures from an interested report and a history; not returns. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Mahan says the city lay between the swamps and the Mississippi with a single narrow land exit, and that the river, full to the tops of the levees, let the fleet's guns command the exit and the streets. Lovell says the high water left the Chalmette lines untenable against guns that looked down on the country, and that one ship at Kenner could command the Jackson Railroad.
claims.rationale: Ground and water described by a history and an interested report; no map verification. The river's height predates the action.

claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from an interested report and a history; the March 22 letter itself was not inspected.

claims.value: NPS and Mahan say Farragut demanded the city's surrender on the 25th and the hoisting of the United States flag. Lovell says he went to the city to remove troops and stores, refused to surrender, and said he would evacuate and turn the city over to the mayor rather than subject it to bombardment.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from a summary, a history and an interested report.

claims.value: Lovell ordered M. L. Smith, commanding the interior lines, to resist at the batteries below the city, and regretted that he had no control of the defenses afloat. Mahan says Farragut sent 250 marines ashore on the 29th and that the city was turned over to Butler on the evening of May 1; NPS says Butler's army began landing that day. The frozen commanders are Major General Mansfield Lovell, Flag Officer David G. Farragut and Major General Benjamin Franklin Butler; the live page gives Farragut as Admiral and does not list Butler.
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report, a history and a summary; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Union victory and the live result Union Victory. NPS says the city surrendered on April 28. Mahan says the mayor announced his submission and Bailey hoisted the flag on the mint, which citizens hauled down the next day; Lovell says he advised the mayor not to surrender the city. Both Lovell and Mahan say the city's fate was decided at the forts.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The form and date of the city's surrender differ between the summary and the inspected accounts.

open_questions: Butler's No. 1 reports, M. L. Smith's report on the Chalmette lines (No. 7), Lovell's inclosures A-D and the Court of Inquiry (No. 8), Farragut's and Bailey's naval reports and the city correspondence remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. A. T. Mahan's The Gulf and Inland Waters (Scribner's, copyright 1883; the Project Gutenberg text of the 1898 London issue) is an interested Union naval history already registered for the Mississippi pass; it relies chiefly on the official reports and cites the Confederate officers' testimony, so it is not independent of them. Lovell's April 26 and May 22, 1862 reports are one interested Confederate family. Official Records Series I, Volume VI is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
